en.body:
## A Glimpse into the Enchanted and the Terrifying

**Wildwood**, the latest cinematic offering from the masters of stop-motion at **LAIKA**, has arrived, and it’s a breathtaking spectacle that defies easy categorization. Directed by **Travis Knight**, this adaptation of **Colin Meloy**’s YA novel plunges viewers into a world where enchantment and terror walk hand-in-hand. While the studio's first film, **Coraline**, cemented an expectation for outright horror, **Wildwood** proves that **LAIKA**’s vision has evolved. The film doesn't shy away from unsettling imagery, opening with a startling sequence that reveals an automaton’s inner workings and later evoking the chilling menace of Hitchcock’s **The Birds** with a swarm of crows menacing children.

This isn't just a horror film; it's a grand, ambitious fantasy epic. **LAIKA** has consistently pushed the boundaries of stop-motion animation, with past films like **Missing Link** aiming for ambitious, genre-reviving adventures. **Wildwood** continues this trend, offering a visual feast that is both meticulously handcrafted and wildly imaginative. The story follows a young girl's journey into a mysterious, magical forest, encountering anthropomorphic armies and navigating a world far darker and more complex than typical children's fare. It’s a modern-day fable, drawing more from the Brothers Grimm and Tolkien than Disney, and it doesn't compromise its vision for younger audiences.

## A Tale for the Passionate Fan

For fans of **LAIKA** and ambitious animation, **Wildwood** represents a significant achievement. The film’s PG-13 rating hints at its mature themes, and the critical reception so far has praised its visual artistry and handcrafted nature. While some critics have noted occasional narrative stumbles, the sheer scale and beauty of the animation are undeniable. This is a film that demands attention, offering a rich, immersive experience that appeals to both seasoned cinephiles and those new to the world of intricate stop-motion storytelling. It’s a testament to the power of handmade cinema in an increasingly digital world, proving that magic can indeed be found in the details.

## What's Next

Having premiered at the 2026 BFI London Film Festival, **Wildwood** is set to captivate audiences in theaters starting October 23. With its stunning visuals and unique blend of fantasy and peril, it's a must-see for anyone who appreciates groundbreaking animation and compelling storytelling.

content_raw: Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 BFI London coverage. The film opens in theaters on October 23. Because of Coraline , LAIKA’s first effort as a studio and still its best-known, there’s an expectation that each subsequent project will fit comfortably within the horror realm, each new release a rite of passage for thousands of kids previously unaware that movies could give them nightmares. This will inevitably be the same case with Wildwood , director Travis Knight’s lavish and ambitious adaptation of the 2011 YA novel by Decemberists lead singer Colin Meloy, not least because it cold-opens with a young boy committing suicide, ripping out his insides to reveal he was an automaton operated by cogs. The gothic imagery hardly subsides from there, with Knight soon recreating the haunting image from Hitchcock’s The Birds , a murder of crows swarming over a playground ready to feast on unsuspecting children. Labelling a LAIKA production a straightforward riff on horror hasn’t been accurate since 2012’s Paranorman ––their weakest, most surface-level referential effort––with the studio’s work since then better appreciated as part of an ongoing attempt to revive other genres unfashionable with today’s kids. It’s won them as much acclaim as it has come at a cost; Missing Link , their 2019 globe-trotting adventure that’s partway between Jules Verne and The Lost City of Z , holds the title for most expensive stop-motion film of all-time, and made the smallest fraction of that cost back.  Wildwood might be an easier sell as a modern-day fairytale, but it doesn’t make any concessions to what children might want or expect from such a proposition—more Brothers Grimm by way of Tolkien than Disney. If it does have a contemporary parallel, it’s with the equally dark, unsanitized female empowerment tales of Hayao Miyazaki, where wonder and grimness co-exist as they did in the oldest bedtime stories. Characters are shaped forever by the darkness they encounter as much as they are thrilled by any fantastical, otherworldly creatures who cross their path, all of whom are crafted with an attention to detail unrivaled within their respective forms of animation.
